title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: price increase
drivers.evidence: Price rose to $2.85 (+5.6%) in the past two weeks (Easter, Apr 6). Sales dropped to 6 and 9 units, respectively (vs baseline 9.5). Average sales in these weeks: 7.5, 19% below baseline. No prior price increase showed lift; past price hikes correlate with lower demand.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 9.5. No events or promotions are scheduled for the target week. The price is increased to $2.85 (+5.6% vs regular $2.70), which is likely to suppress demand. Past price increases (e.g., Easter week) show no lift; in fact, Easter week saw a drop to 6 units (vs baseline 9.5). The historical trend shows a sharp decline (-42.6% over 13 weeks), and recent weeks (Mar–Apr) average 7.5 units, below baseline. The classical uplift model suggests no effect, but price increases are a known demand reducer. Evidence is strong enough to adjust downward. Noise-adjusted effect of price hikes is not significant, but consistent underperformance post-price change supports a downward bias. The median is adjusted to reflect expected decline.

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-81% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
